children: ‎Kenya will use a staggering Ksh2.4 trillion ($18.6 billion) to pay some 300,000 public service retirees, according to the National Treasury, reflecting the monumental burden on the country's national budget.‎‎The latest disclosures on public pension liability are part of the ongoing valuation of public assets and liabilities, as the government transitions from cash-based to accrual system of accounting. The valuation began on July 1, 2026.

Jonah Wala, National Treasury’s director in charge of Accounting Services, told The EastAfrican that they are looking for assets to support the pensions bill.‎The massive pension liability accounts for 18.46 percent of the current national debt of Ksh13 trillion ($100.77 billion) and 50 percent of the current national budget of Ksh4.82 trillion ($37.36 billion) for the 2026/2027 fiscal year.‎‎It emanates from the old government pension plan, which guaranteed fixed lifetime payouts to former civil servants, teachers, and security officers, ‎reflecting the fiscal strain on government resources amid mounting expenditure pressures.

But Treasury says there is an elaborate plan in place to manage the huge pension liability without putting undue pressure on an exchequer already weighed down by mounting expenditure and salary increment demands from teachers, lecturers, and health workers.“We have strategies to come up with income-generating assets that will help us to pay those pensioners so that we manage the risk of paying somebody from the exchequer until he dies,” Mr Wala said.
These will include investments in income-generating properties, infrastructure and government securities.

The new Public Service Superannuation Fund (PSSF) requires workers to save for themselves. The government-backed fund runs a defined contribution pension scheme for Kenyan public servants, which came into force on January 1, 2021.

The National Treasury started valuing assets owned by the public from July 1, marking the last part of its transition to a new financial reporting standard that recognises income after it is earned and expenses that have already been incurred irrespective of the actual cash movement.‎‎State corporations have already shifted to accrual accounting from cash-based accounting and the assets in these corporations have already been accounted for.‎‎Cabinet approved the transition to accrual accounting from cash accounting on March 7, 2024 and in August the same year, the National Treasury assembled a steering committee to oversee the transition.

‎‎In February 2025, the Treasury approved valuation of all assets that Kenya owns as part of the move to shift the government's operations to a new reporting plan by 2027‎‎The government set a three-year roadmap to consolidate all government assets and liabilities into a single balance sheet that shows the state's true financial position and help save on foreign borrowing.

‎‎Treasury says the policy shift will improve transparency in the management of public debt and pending bills and help the government negotiate cheaper loans from foreign lenders.‎‎Under the accrual accounting system, the government will record all borrowing by the state and provide full disclosures on key details, including linking the proceeds of the loans to respective projects.‎‎

Currently, pending bills, pension liabilities and public debt are not recorded in government books but in separate government registers, a move that has, for instance, made it difficult to relate public debt to projects.‎‎Accrual accounting therefore offers a more comprehensive picture of the government's financial health.janyanzwa@ke.nationmedia.com

title: ZAWYA: Kenyan Treasury struggles with $18bln pensions bill
